about: Input for narration: see scenes/NARRATION.md. Key every line to statement ids; record contentHash.
scope: the campaign around the battle: steps 1-4 lead to it, 12-13 follow it and belong to other events

bases.sourced: a stored passage says it; the quotation is verbatim
bases.inferred: joined up from sourced points; 'by' says whose inference
bases.illustrative: drawn so the picture reads; no passage (a Generalized Abstraction, D-172)
bases.not-checked: the passage it rests on is not held yet; 'by' says who asserted it

subject: Battle of Actium

steps.title: Antony holds the coast of western Greece

statements.text: Antony sails back to the Peloponnese and winters at Patrae.

voices.quotation: he sailed back to the Peloponnesus, the season being already late autumn, and passed the winter at Patrae

statements.text: He spreads his soldiers to guard the strategic points and secure provisions.

voices.quotation: distributing his soldiers in every direction in order that they might keep guard over the strategic points and secure more easily an abundance of provisions

statements.text: Antony's garrisons hold Corcyra.

voices.quotation: seized Corcyra, which had been deserted by the garrisons there

statements.text: Antony holds Methone.

voices.quotation: Agrippa had captured Methone by storm

statements.note: Implied: Agrippa had to take it from Antony.

statements.text: The chain of posts guards the supply route from Egypt.
statements.by: the animation's generator (Claude, in a chat, from Wikipedia and its own knowledge)
statements.note: Dio gives guard and provisions; Egypt as the route is the generator's.

statements.text: Agrippa takes Methone by storm and kills Bogud there.

voices.quotation: Agrippa had captured Methone by storm and killed Bogud there

statements.text: From there he watches for the merchant ships and raids the coasts of Greece.

voices.quotation: was now watching for the merchant vessels that came to land and was making descents from time to time on various parts of Greece

statements.text: The merchant ships were grain ships from Egypt.
statements.by: the animation's generator (Claude, in a chat, from Wikipedia and its own knowledge)
statements.note: Dio says merchant vessels; Egypt and grain are not in the passage.

statements.text: Octavian crosses the Ionian Gulf from Brundisium with his whole force.

voices.quotation: Thereupon he crossed the Ionian Gulf with the entire array

statements.text: His cavalry lands at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains.

voices.quotation: Caesar disembarked the cavalry at the foot of the Ceraunian mountains

statements.text: He seizes Corcyra, abandoned by its garrisons.

voices.quotation: seized Corcyra, which had been deserted by the garrisons there

statements.text: He occupies Toryne in Epirus.

voices.quotation: occupying a place in Epeirus called Torun

statements.text: He camps on the high ground north of the strait, where Nicopolis later stood.

voices.quotation: He then occupied the site where Nicopolis now stands
took up a position on high ground there

statements.text: He marches south from Toryne to the camp.
statements.by: the animation's generator (Claude, in a chat, from Wikipedia and its own knowledge)

statements.text: Agrippa takes Leucas, takes Patrae after beating Nasidius at sea, and later takes Corinth.

voices.quotation: Agrippa made a sudden dash with his fleet and captured Leucas and the vessels which were there, took Patrae by conquering Quintus Nasidius in a sea-fight, and later reduced Corinth also
Marcus Agrippa had stormed Leucas, had captured Patrae, had seized Corinth

statements.text: Antony's forces lose men to disease and desertion.

voices.quotation: their numbers had been diminished by disease and desertions
from Antony to Caesar someone or other was deserting daily

statements.text: Cut off from bringing in grain, Antony's provisions begin to fail.

voices.quotation: when provisions also began to fail him because he was shut off from bringing in grain

steps.title: The fleets form up outside the strait

statements.text: The battle is fought on 2 September.

voices.quotation: Such was the naval battle in which they engaged on the second of September

statements.text: Antony's fleet draws up its line a little outside the strait and comes no further.

voices.quotation: drew up their line a little outside the strait and advanced no further

statements.text: Antony orders his ships to hold their position at the narrow mouth of the gulf.

voices.quotation: to maintain their position at the mouth of the gulf, which was narrow and difficult

statements.text: Octavian keeps his ships about eight furlongs (some 1.5 km) away, waiting a long time.

voices.quotation: kept his own ships at a distance of about eight furlongs from the enemy
ordered his sailors to let their oars rest in the water, and waited for a time

statements.note: 1.5 km is the conversion; west of Antony's line is the map's.

statements.text: Cleopatra's sixty ships lie behind the line.

voices.quotation: they had been posted in the rear of the large vessels
Cleopatra, riding at anchor behind the combatants

statements.note: Both sources say the rear; 'behind the centre', as the animation had it, is ours, and the map draws it so.

ordersOfBattle.title: Three orders of battle
ordersOfBattle.note: The sources disagree: two ancient versions and a modern summary that combines them, shown side by side, never merged. The map draws one arrangement: a reconstruction (curator, 2026-11-25).

voices.quotation: Antony had the right wing, with Publicola, Coelius the left, and in the centre were Marcus Octavius and Marcus Insteius
Caesar posted Agrippa on the left, and reserved the right wing for himself

alternatives.note: Plutarch names no commander for Octavian's centre. That Antony's centre engaged Arruntius (66.3) comes later in the fight; it is not his order of battle.

voices.quotation: The command of the right wing of Caesar's fleet was entrusted to Marcus Lurius, of the left to Arruntius, while Agrippa had full charge of the entire conflict at sea
The command of Antony's fleet was entrusted to Publicola and Sosius

alternatives.note: Velleius gives Sosius no wing; the animation's 'Coelius south (Velleius: Sosius)' was its generator's reading.

alternatives.accordingTo: Wikipedia, Battle of Actium (a modern summary)

voices.quotation: led by the experienced admiral Agrippa, commanding from the left wing of the fleet, Lucius Arruntius the centre, and Marcus Lurius the right
Marcus Octavius and Marcus Insteius commanded the centre, while Gaius Sosius commanded the left wing

alternatives.note: It combines the two: Plutarch's Antonian right and centre, Velleius's Arruntius and Lurius, and a left wing for Sosius that neither ancient passage held gives.

statements.text: At the sixth hour, with a wind rising from the sea, Antony's men put their left wing in motion.

voices.quotation: it was now the sixth hour, and since a wind was rising from the sea, the soldiers of Antony became impatient at the delay

statements.text: Octavian orders his right wing to row backwards, to draw them out of the gulf and the narrows.

voices.quotation: ordered his right wing to row backwards, wishing to draw the enemy still farther out from the gulf and the narrows

statements.text: Agrippa extends his wing to encircle; Publicola advances against him and is cut off from the centre.

voices.quotation: as Agrippa was extending the left wing with a view to encircling the enemy, Publicola was forced to advance against him, and so was separated from the centre

statements.text: Antony's centre falls into confusion, engaging Arruntius.

voices.quotation: The centre falling into confusion and engaging with Arruntius

statements.text: This happens on the northern side of the battle.
statements.by: the animation's generator (Claude, in a chat, from Wikipedia and its own knowledge)
statements.note: Agrippa held Octavian's left (Plutarch), which faced north as the fleets lay; the compass point is ours.

statements.text: Cleopatra's sixty ships hoist their sails and make off through the midst of the fighting.

voices.quotation: suddenly the sixty ships of Cleopatra were seen hoisting their sails for flight and making off through the midst of the combatants

statements.text: They take advantage of the wind and make for the Peloponnese.

voices.quotation: they took advantage of the wind and made for Peloponnesus

statements.text: She turns to flight from the strain of waiting, and signals her ships.

voices.quotation: she suddenly turned to flight herself and raised the signal for the others

statements.note: Dio's reading: panic. Whether the flight was planned is a debated Question in the graph.

statements.text: Velleius puts it on her: Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight, and Antony chose to go with her rather than stay with his fighting men.

voices.quotation: Cleopatra took the initiative in the flight; Antony chose to be the companion of the fleeing queen rather than of his fighting soldiers

statements.note: One interpretation: the victors' side of the story, told by a soldier of the next reign. Shown beside Dio's panic and the planned-breakout reading, not over them.

disputed.words: Panic, her initiative, or a planned breakout?

questions.label: Did Cleopatra, and perhaps Antonius too, secretly plan the flight before the battle began?
Did Cleopatra take the decisive initiative in the flight from Actium?
Did Cleopatra's squadron escape from the battle through a gap in the fleets' line?

statements.text: Antony leaves the fight in a five-oared galley, with only Alexas the Syrian and Scellius, and goes after her.

voices.quotation: got into a five-oared galley, where Alexas the Syrian and Scellius were his only companions, and hastened after the woman

statements.text: Dio: he thought her ships fled from fear, not at her bidding, and so followed.

voices.quotation: Antony thought they were fleeing, not at the bidding of Cleopatra, but through fear because they felt themselves vanquished, and so he followed them

statements.text: The fleet left behind loses its commander.
statements.by: the check of 2026-11-24 (Claude Code, against the stored passages)

questions.label: Did Cleopatra, and perhaps Antonius too, secretly plan the flight before the battle began?

corrected.was: The fleet loses its commander, its reserve and its treasury.
corrected.why: Dio says the money was still aboard the ships left fighting: Octavian held back from fire to gain it.

voices.quotation: Previously he had wished to avoid using it, in order to gain possession of the money
in the hope that they might possibly gain possession of the money

steps.title: The fleet left behind is destroyed
steps.timeWords: late afternoon, to the tenth hour

statements.text: With the fight still even, Octavian sends to the camp for fire.

voices.quotation: As the fight continued equal, Caesar, at a loss what he should do, sent for fire from the camp

statements.text: His ships attack from many sides with blazing missiles, torches and pots of charcoal and pitch.

voices.quotation: The assailants would approach their victims from many directions at once

statements.text: Antony's fleet holds out until the tenth hour, worn down by a rising sea; three hundred ships are captured.

voices.quotation: only after it had been most severely damaged by the high sea which rose against it did it reluctantly, and at the tenth hour, give up the struggle
three hundred ships were captured, as Caesar himself has written

statements.note: Plutarch and Dio differ on what ended it: the sea, or the fire. Both are kept.

steps.title: The army goes over without fighting

statements.text: Antony's legions hold together for seven days, ignoring Octavian's messages.

voices.quotation: they held together for seven days, paying no heed to the messages which Caesar sent them

statements.text: Then Canidius runs away by night, and the army goes over to Octavian.

voices.quotation: after Canidius their general had run away by night and forsaken the camp, being now destitute of all things and betrayed by their commanders, they went over to the conqueror

corrected.was: Canidius slips away. After seven days the legions go over.
corrected.why: Plutarch has the seven days first, and Canidius's flight at their end.

steps.title: Flight to Taenarum, then Egypt
steps.context: after the battle (outside the event's phases)

statements.text: Antony is taken aboard Cleopatra's ship.

voices.quotation: Antony came up and was taken on board

statements.text: He means to cross from Taenarum to Libya.

voices.quotation: he purposed to cross from Taenarum to Libya

statements.text: They go as far as the Peloponnese together; Cleopatra then hastens to Egypt.

voices.quotation: had gone as far as the Peloponnesus together
Cleopatra had hastened to Egypt

statements.text: Antony reaches the coast of Libya and sends Cleopatra on into Egypt from Paraetonium.

voices.quotation: After Antony had reached the coast of Libya and sent Cleopatra forward into Egypt from Paraetonium

statements.text: Antony is at Paraetonium until the news of Pelusium.

voices.quotation: At the news concerning Pelusium Antony returned from Paraetonium

routes.note: Where Cleopatra parted from Antony: the sources differ, and both are kept.

alternatives.words: She went with him to Libya and on into Egypt from Paraetonium.

voices.quotation: sent Cleopatra forward into Egypt from Paraetonium

alternatives.words: From the Peloponnese she hastened to Egypt.

voices.quotation: had gone as far as the Peloponnesus together
Cleopatra had hastened to Egypt

steps.title: Alexandria falls
steps.context: the end of the war (another event)

statements.text: Antony's fleet goes over to Octavian before Alexandria.

voices.quotation: on their returning the salute changed sides
Cleopatra, upon perceiving this, caused the ships to desert

statements.note: Plutarch tells it as the crews' own choice; Dio has Cleopatra cause it. Both are kept.

statements.text: His cavalry deserts, his infantry is beaten, and he retires into the city.

voices.quotation: he was deserted by his cavalry, which went over to the enemy, and after being defeated with his infantry he retired into the city

statements.text: Told that Cleopatra is dead, Antony wounds himself, and dies with her in the tomb.

voices.quotation: Antony believed the message
gave himself a wound and fell upon his face
So Antony died there in Cleopatra's bosom

statements.text: Octavian drives into the city.

voices.quotation: And now Caesar himself drove into the city

statements.text: The city fell on 1 August 30 BC.
statements.by: the animation's generator (Claude, in a chat, from Wikipedia and its own knowledge)
statements.note: No passage read gives the date. Dio 51.19.6 says the day of the capture was declared a lucky day, without naming it.

statements.text: Cleopatra dies; Octavian admires her spirit and has her buried with Antony.

voices.quotation: he gave orders that her body should be buried with that of Antony in splendid and regal fashion

statements.text: Octavian now holds all power alone.

voices.quotation: Caesar now for the first time held all the power alone

statements.note: Dio dates this from Actium, not from Alexandria.
